utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Misetic or Mr. Kehoe, is the Gotovina Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just announce right now, to give the Prosecution an opportunity. At the conclusion of the 92 ter submissions, I intend to tender four documents on the basis that they're mentioned in the statement, and these would be 65 ter 2336, 65 ter 3518, 65 ter 667, and 65 ter 3089. All of them are laws that the witness mentions in the early part of his statements, and I don't intend to cover them in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were already on your 65 ter list, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Matulovic. If you would look in this direction, then you know who's talking. Yes. Good morning. Mr. Matulovic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Matulovic. Mr. Matulovic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Mr. Misetic, and Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Misetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Matulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Matulovic, do you recall meeting with representatives of the Gotovina Defence on the 31st of March, 2006; the 12th of February, 2007; and the 20th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to see the witness statement that you signed on the 26th of May, 2009, on the basis of the discussions in those interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, Madam Usher, I'd like to hand you a copy of the statement in Croatian. And also, Madam Registrar, if we could have on the screen, please, 1D2697.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Matulovic, I note that in proofing for today's session, you had a correction to make in paragraph 1 of the statement. If you could explain to the Court what the correction is in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I corrected in paragraph 1 was the manner of appointment of judges to military courts within operations zones. Upon the proposal of the defence minister and in accordance with the war assignment, we were appointed by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could clarify. On whose proposal was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Other than that correction, is there anything else that needs to be corrected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Not for the time being, I don't think there is anything else to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the time you gave this statement to the members of the Gotovina Defence, did you give your answers to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today that you were asked by members of the Gotovina Defence, would you provide the same answers today in court as you provided in the witness statement that's on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I would provide exactly the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And one more thing. Madam Registrar, if you could go to the first page of the exhibit, please. Is that -- in the bottom right-hand corner, Mr. Matulovic, do you recognise your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D2697 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1613 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1013"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Now I would like to tender four exhibits that are referenced in the statement. These exhibits are 65 ter 2336, 65 ter 3518, 65 ter 667, and 65 ter 3089.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Madam Registrar, the numbers would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1614 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1014"], D1615, D1616, and D1617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1014 through D1017 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please repeat the numbers, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers are D1614 through D1617.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I missed that. So therefore instead of D1014 through D1017, instead of those numbers that are, of course, already in evidence, D1614 through D1617 are admitted into evidence. I notice that it appears twice in the transcript, and that is where the Registrar, mentioned the numbers, whereas the last numbers I mentioned are the correct ones. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just point out, the statement has -- it's recorded as D1013. I presume it should be 1613, going by the correction that was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And reference is made to page 4, line 21, where also apparently by mistake, "D1013" should be "D1613." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have explained to the witness the procedure concerning reading the summary, and with your leave, I would like to read out a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness Zoran Matulovic is a trial judge in the Criminal Department of the County Court in Split. From 1992 through December 1996, Judge Matulovic was a judge at the Military Court in Split, and throughout 1995 he was the president of the Military Court in Split. In his statement, Judge Matulovic describes some of the laws that govern the work of the military courts, including the scope of their jurisdiction. Oversight of the work of the military courts was conducted by the Ministry of Justice, to which the military courts would send reports concerning the results of their work. After Operation Storm, the military courts sent reports of their work to the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in intervals of every 15 days. If the military courts were not properly carrying out their tasks, the Ministry of Justice would be required to take appropriate steps to correct the problem. Judge Matulovic also testifies that the military courts did not have jurisdiction to try war crimes cases. In cases where the perpetrator of a crime is unknown, the investigation of the crime is always conducted by the investigating judge of the civilian District Court. The investigating judge of the Military Court joins the investigation at the moment it has been established that the perpetrator of the criminal offence is a soldier. Judge Matulovic testifies that it was not possible for a military commander to influence the work of the military courts. He also states that the State Attorney's Office and the Military Prosecutor's Office could institute preliminary criminal procedures on the basis of any available information concerning the perpetration of a criminal offence, including on the basis of information obtained from the media. Mr. President, that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Matulovic, I'm going to ask you now a few questions based on the answers you gave in your witness statement. First, if you could tell the Court, how many judges were in the Military Court in August of 1995, for the Split Military Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Decree on Establishing Military Courts within operations zones, it was stated that military courts shall have a president of the court, who is also a trial judge, and four judges. The Military Courts in Split had a very broad territorial jurisdiction, so we also had three judges in Zadar, Dubrovnik, and Sibenik, who belonged to the courts, so a total of eight judges worked with the Military Court in Split. These judges that worked elsewhere mostly conducted on-site investigations, and then, where practicable, they were also a member of the panel of judges, because all of these judges were professional judges, and the panels always tried cases where the envisaged sentence was above five years of imprisonment, whereas a single judge would try cases where the maximum sentence was under five years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question. Can you tell the Court, then, in the cases where the maximum sentence was below five years, what the appellate court -- where that case would be appealed to after the judgement of the Military Court judge, and in cases where the maximum sentence was in excess of five years, where would the appeal jurisdiction lie for such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: If the Military Court handed down a judgement or, rather, if a judgement was handed by a single judge, then appeal from that judgement would be submitted to the District Court in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in cases tried by the three-judge panel for crimes with a maximum sentence in excess of five years, which court would hear the appeal from such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: In those cases, the appeal would be filed before the Supreme Court of Croatia, as the highest court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any such things as military appellate courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: They never existed within the then system of military courts. Initially, at the beginning of my testimony, I said that the military courts were under the direct responsibility of the Ministry of Justice, which is to say that these military courts were not subordinated to any other body within the military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Matulovic, turning your attention to paragraphs 9 and 10 of your statement, can you explain to the Court your answer that the investigative judge of the Military Court joins the investigation at the moment it has been established beyond doubt that the perpetrator of the criminal offence is a soldier? Let me ask you: Can you explain to the Court, if a crime is committed and there's a possibility that it was committed by an HV member, explain to the Court what the procedure is to get the military court involved. In other words, at what stage would the military court be involved if there is merely a suspicion that an HV soldier committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure on involving the military judge or the Military Court, after a crime was perpetrated, was identical as in relation to the civilian courts, which is to say that it was regulated on the decree on applying the Law on Criminal Procedure. It was the old Law on Criminal Procedure, but it was reduced, as we used to say, in some chapters so as to be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think I didn't put my question well, so let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a military judge was on duty, then he would be informed either by a civilian or military police that a crime was perpetrated. The civilian police always inform the judge whenever it wasn't possible to establish with certainty the status of the perpetrator, whether he was a soldier or not. If this was an urgent case, and going out for an on-site investigation is considered an urgent case, when the status of the perpetrator or a suspect wasn't possible to establish, then a civilian judge would go out to carry out on-site investigation. If they could establish that the perpetrator or a suspect was a soldier, then a military judge would go out to conduct on-site investigation and then would continue on together with the military prosecutor. So in order to carry out an on-site investigation or in order to carry out any urgent investigative measure, it was important to establish, at the moment the information was received, to establish with certainty that the suspect was a military serviceman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there any circumstance in which the Military Court would have jurisdiction over a crime where the perpetrator is unknown?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is precisely what I just spoke about. Only in cases where they knew that the crime was committed by a military service person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to -- continuing on this issue of jurisdiction of the military courts, can you explain to the Court, if a crime was committed by a member of the HV, but he was -- he left the HV for whatever reason between the time of the commission of the offence and the bringing of the indictment, which court would have jurisdiction, the civilian or the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Now we come into the second stage of the criminal procedure, which is to say that investigation had been conducted and we now come to the stage when an indictment is to be issued. At the moment when an indictment is issued, it was very important to know whether the person who now is becoming an indictee is still a member of the HV or not. If -- cases where that person was demobilised before the indictment was issued by the Court, then the case would fall under the jurisdiction of civilian courts. For example, let me give you an example. A murder was committed. At the time the murder was committed -- I apologise. At the time the murder was committed, the perpetrator was in the military, serving in the military, so the investigation is commenced and conducted by a military investigating judge. After the investigation is completed, the case is sent to the military prosecutor, and then it is the military prosecutor who issues the indictment if the person is still a soldier. If the perpetrator is not in the military, then automatically the case would be sent to the civilian courts for indictment, and then the civilian courts would continue to proceed with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Following up on your last answer, if, after the conclusion of the work of the military investigative judge, jurisdiction changed to the civilian courts, would the civilian courts have to start all over in the investigation, or would the military judge turn over the file to the civilian court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood. The procedure is continued exactly where it was halted within the military system, so the case would be sent to the public -- civilian prosecutor, and not a single stage of the proceedings would be repeated. They would just continue it where they left it off in the previous system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1333.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Matulovic, this is a decree issued by President Tudjman on the 30th of November, 1992. If we could scroll down to Article 1, the last sentence, it says: "After paragraph 1, the new paragraph 2 is added, reading: 'Exceptionally, if the perpetrator of the crimes in criminal cases under items 1 and 4, paragraph 1, of this Article has ceased to be an active serviceman before an indictment is issued, the trial will be carried out before the competent Municipal or District Court.'" Is this the basis upon which your answer is based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I have just told you. You see, regardless of the stage of proceedings where the status was changed, the case would be turned over to the civilian courts, and especially at the time -- at the stage of proceedings where an indictment is about to be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 1333 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D1618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1618 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 of your statement, you state that the Military Court submits reports on its work to the Ministry of Justice and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia. Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber, if there was a problem in the functioning of the military court system, was it the Ministry of Justice that would review the work and propose solutions to any problems in the functioning of the military court system?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice is part of administration, and it is duty-bound to provide everything that all courts need in order to carry out their regular functioning, try cases, have proceedings, and so on. So it was exclusively the Ministry of Justice that was responsible for taking care of the work of military courts, and the military courts would send reports to the cases they have completed, to the duties of justice, to any cases where Statutes of Limitation had run out. So everything that the judges did was under the scrutiny of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to paragraph 11 of your statement. This is where you were asked: "Was it possible that a military commander could influence the work of the Military Court? If so, in what way?" And your answer was: "In no way could a military commander influence the work of the Military Court." Now, I'd like to show you a document that's been admitted into evidence and that was sent to you. And if we could go to Exhibit P2251, please. This is one example of a daily report that would be sent by the Duty Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and it lists events, crimes, disciplinary infractions -- or breaches, I should say. And if we could turn to the second-to-last page in this document, please. And you can see that it was delivered to, amongst others, at number 6, to the Military Court of the Split Military District and, number 7, to the Military Prosecutor's Office. Can you explain to the Court, what was your understanding of why you were receiving copies of the daily reports of the duty service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise at the beginning, on the last page which we cannot see now, but if you pay attention, you will see that the report was signed by the head of shift of the military police, and this provides the answer as to why they had to send it, because the military police, just like the civilian police, works 24 hours a day, and the head of the shift is responsible for sending the report to everyone listed here. And the report contains also the report about infractions of military discipline, whether these were just minor infractions or violations of discipline; then also information about any crimes that may have been committed during the shift, and other items. Why it was sent to the Military Court of the Split Military District, we required the 72nd Battalion of Military Police to submit it to us, but I wish to say that the reason why we requested this, reports like this one, was that the judge who was on duty, the investigative judge, would, on the next day, when he would transfer his duty to somebody else, would have an insight into what had been going on. And essentially in this way, military judges were able to control the work of military police and made sure that the reports were sent duly and regularly to court. So it shouldn't happen that in the area of their responsibility or jurisdiction, anything should happen without the investigative judge or prosecutor knowing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Explain, then, if something appeared in the daily report, for example, a crime, and the duty judge received a copy of the daily report and noted that he hadn't been notified, prior to this, that the crime had been committed, what steps would be taken by the Court or by the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: For further steps, if a crime was committed - I'm just speaking generally - the military prosecutor would be in charge. In our system, the military judge and the Military Court cannot do anything on their own initiative because the proceedings are launched and then further conducted by the military prosecutor. If there was an omission of something in the report, then we would inform both the commander of the 72nd Battalion and also the highest officer of military police about this, because the person who was the head of the shift was in charge of this. I may also add that I do not remember that we had such problems at the Military Court in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you note, number 2 there, is -- it's also given to the commander of the Split Military District, and 3 is commander of the Split Garrison. Did you have an understanding -- or did the commander of the Split Military District have a role in controlling the work of the military crime police concerning the commission of criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't really have a role because the military police was being administered by the military police. And as for submitting reports under items 2 or 3 to the commander of the Split Military District and the Split Garrison of this report, the answer is contained in what I have told you earlier; namely, that the reports, if you have a closer look at them, also mention all the violations of military discipline, and it's normal that within the military subordination system both the commander of the Split Military District and the Split Garrison must know if there were any infractions of discipline in the units. They must know that this happened. And I emphasise that the military disciplinary proceedings and also the criminal proceedings, if they followed from these reports, that anything needed to be conducted, had nothing to do one with the other. These were separate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, as the president of the Military Court in Split at all times relevant to the indictment period here, did General Gotovina have the ability, as far as you knew, to influence the criminal -- military criminal justice system from the time of investigation all the way through the time of pronouncement of judgement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Considering the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure, according to which both the civilian and military courts proceeded, Mr. Gotovina, as a commander, had absolutely no ability, in terms of the proceedings, to influence the work of the Military Court in any way whatsoever, or the Military Prosecutor's Office, for that matter. And let me add that in these five years I personally never heard that anyone called him or that he called anyone if some matter was in the jurisdiction of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the five years that you were in the Military Court in Split?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, until the 6th of December, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a meeting that was held in the Ministry of Defence in October of 1995. If we turn first to 65 ter 1D2784, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. President, I'm advised that I need to seek leave to add this exhibit to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This was an invitation that was sent to various addresses, including the Military Court, all presidents of the Military Court, concerning a working session that was to be held on the 19th of October, 1995, at 1100 hours in the Ministry of Defence. The topics to be discussed were: Problems faced by military courts and Military State Prosecutor's Offices in their work regarding the legal obligations of the Ministry of Defence and the Croatian Army, particularly after Operations Flash and Storm. The second point was suggestions and requests from military courts and Military State Prosecutor's Offices. And there were two other points. Do you recall receiving this invitation to attend the meeting on the 19th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I received this invitation, and I attended this meeting. As you can see, the invitation was made at the Defence Ministry. The deputy minister, who was then Mr. Juras, was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that Exhibit 65 ter 1D2784 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1619 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 4656, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is dated 20 October 1995, and it was sent from the Ministry of Defence to all presidents of the military courts, amongst other people as well. If we turn the page in the English, please. And this is the cover letter submitting the conclusions reached at the working session on the 19th October 1995. And now if we could go to the actual conclusions, which is 65 ter 1D2785, please. I'm advised that I need to seek leave to add this document as well, Mr. President, to the 65 ter exhibit list. This is, again, 65 ter 1D2785.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The report -- you say that you attended the meeting. It says these are the conclusions that were reached at the meeting, and the first conclusion is: "It is the unanimous opinion of the participants at the working session that the work of the military courts and the military Prosecutor's offices has contributed in an effective manner to the functioning and protection of the law-based state, the Republic of Croatia." And if we go to point 8 of the document, it says: "It is the unanimous opinion of the participants at the working session that the law-based state has functioned effectively in the liberated area of the Republic of Croatia during the actions Flash and Storm, and the accusations of the ill-intentioned internal and external factors against the Croatian state and the Croatian Army are groundless, since the competent organs of authorities have fulfilled their legal obligations on time and in an efficient manner." Can you explain to the Court what was meant when that conclusion was reached? In other words, can you explain to the Court what the participants at the meeting felt concerning the effectiveness of the criminal -- military criminal justice system after Operation Storm up until the time of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, on the first page of these conclusions it's mentioned there that after the meeting was held, the conclusions were made by the Legal Affairs Administration, and therefore I can interpret this conclusion which I mentioned in the way that I understood it, and later on I saw that it really was like that. You know that the responsibility of military courts included the crimes from Article 20 of the Criminal Code, and these were the crimes that related to the protection of facilities where this related to the Republic of Croatia, its territorial integrity and everything else connected with this. The military courts were -- had the jurisdiction for these crimes. That was the armed rebellion and also carrying out sabotage and terrorist operations, and the like, everything that was intended to attack the integrity of the Republic of Croatia. After these operations, Flash and Storm, I assert that both the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military courts worked as best they could. All the prisoners were brought before courts in the areas where they had been arrested, and the proceedings were conducted urgently. As a rule, they began by the questioning of these persons, then the investigative procedure followed, and finally the indictments would be issued. I wish to emphasise, and I think that this is very important, that precisely in case of such crimes, if the proceedings were conducted against prisoners, as I said, not a single case that was part of the jurisdiction of the Military Court in Split became a problematic case. What do I mean by this? I think that not a single prisoner was maltreated in any way whatsoever. The proceedings were conducted in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, in accordance with the Criminal Code, and that was the basis for these proceedings. There were many such cases, because we had a large number of prisoners, and therefore I think that this conclusion which was made at the Legal Affairs Administration was well formulated, and that was that the law-based state was very effective in the newly-liberated territories of the Republic of Croatia and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to crimes that were committed after Operation Storm by members of the HV, was it -- what was the conclusion of the participants at the meeting concerning the effectiveness of the military criminal justice system in prosecuting members of the HV who may have committed a crime after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the item 8 of the conclusions related equally to the members of the HV. That means all the proceedings and prosecutions that were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall ever, in a circumstance where any of the participants in the meeting, whether the Military Court, the Military Prosecutor's Office, or any other participant in the meeting, suggested that military commanders needed to take action to prevent crime because the criminal justice system was unable to effectively deal with the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think the answer is suggested in the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at this meeting on the 19th about any problems in the functioning of the military criminal justice system which needed to be handled or addressed by military commanders? Let me rephrase it again. Let's first turn to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer. I understood your question, so if you wish me to answer, I'm willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: This can be connected with something I already talked about; namely, that military commanders, or anyone within the defence system, could not control nor did they have the jurisdiction to influence the work of military courts and Military Prosecutor's Office in specific cases. If there were any problems, if there were any -- I emphasise this. I'm not saying that there were any, but if there were any problems with discipline within units, that was an internal matter to be dealt with the commander of these units. That was at the level of the Defence Ministry and these units and their commanders. So whether the commanders were satisfied or dissatisfied with anything that was conducted was not a matter that was discussed at this meeting, as far as I can remember, because we mostly discussed crimes and criminal offences. That was important, in terms of the public, both the domestic and the international public, because both of these closely monitored the work of these courts and prosecutor's offices through various organisations and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn to paragraph 7 of the conclusions of this meeting. If we can go back one page in English, please. Paragraph 7 on the screen, Judge. It says -- one of the conclusions was: "The Ministry of Defence shall commit all establishment units, the Main Staff, and the commands of the military districts to meet the court requests fully and in a timely manner also regarding the submission of necessary evidence for specific cases. The MUP shall also provide the necessary assistance regarding the submission of evidence." Can you explain to the Court what that conclusion referred to? What was that about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this conclusion related to the work of military police which needed to be updated to a maximum in all cases that were in any way part of the jurisdiction of military courts. When you conduct a complex on-site investigation, apart from the minutes that you have to take, then you also take the traces, you try to find traces of blood and urine, and there are many other activities that need to be carried out and that are very important for the further work of the court in the investigative procedure, and we wanted to have this updated as much as possible. And if an analysis could be made in five days, then one shouldn't wait 15 days for the results, and that related primarily to this kind of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there a problem at all up until this meeting with the cooperation offered by the Main Staff or the commands of military districts in cooperating in criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the cooperation was quite good. There were not any significant problems in the work of the court; perhaps only during one period because the units were at the front, we had minor problems that had to do with delivering subpoenas, and the subpoenas needed to be delivered to military personnel, just like to police personnel. So you didn't have just the first and last name and the place of residence, but the unit. And what happened? The unit would be somewhere in the field, and one person within the unit would be in charge of receiving mail, just as it is now in the police and in the army, and this person was the only one who could sign the receipt of any documents. And at the time these persons, obviously, didn't have a lot of experience in this sort of work, it could happen that they would write on the subpoena that a certain person was at such and such a front-line, and then the subpoena would be returned to the court. The court would then see what the problem was, and this was one minor problem that later on we managed to resolve very efficiently and quickly, and eventually we eliminated it altogether. So it wasn't a major problem that could be interpreted as someone's ill intentions or obstructing the proceedings, but lack of experience or a lack of knowledge of the persons who were in charge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 4656 and 65 ter 1D2785 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits D1620 and D1621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both exhibits are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You've already mentioned, Judge, that your court was processing prisoners of war, and if -- I'd like to show you a document on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I need leave to add 65 ter 1D2786 to our 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if I could have on the screen, please, 65 ter 1D2786, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order from a military judge on the 8th of August. Are you -- do you know Judge Bosko Jurisic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the judges initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is an order that says -- I'm sorry, it's not an order. I guess it's a request, because it goes --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: It's not an order. This is a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A letter asking with respect to where prisoners should be held and in what prisons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this has to do with those who were arrested within the Operation Storm. May I read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: There's all of those who were arrested and against whom there was already issued a decision, putting them in detention, and against whom a warrant was issued, that they should be taken to the District Court in Zadar, regardless of the fact whether the warrant requests that they need to be taken into custody, into other district courts, and so on. So this is something that was written by the military judge, Bosko Jurisic, after the Operation Storm. And the only reason why such orders were issued was to speed up the proceedings as much as possible; that is to say, to reduce any possibility for these people, who were prisoners, to find themselves in some difficult situations, including transport over 200 kilometres and so on, so that they were to be taken to the prison which was closer to the location where they were arrested, and that the proceedings should follow from there. And all of this was done in order to speed up the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask that 65 ter 1D2786 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1622 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Matulovic, may I ask you a question. When Mr. Misetic said to you, This is an order, you immediately corrected him by saying, This is a letter, not an order. Nevertheless, approximately ten lines later, you said such orders were given for those and those purposes. Now, does this letter contain an order that is an instruction which should be followed by the addressee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably said -- you probably didn't hear when, at the beginning, I said this was not an order, because an order implies that something is being ordered. This is a memo with an instruction. So these are two different notions. So the judge here instructs them to proceed in this manner, to the extent possible, and one of the reasons why they wanted it to be done this way was because the prison in Split was over-crowded, so this was a practical solution. And, once again, this was not an order. This was an instruction in the form of a letter or a memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I did notice your answer, unless there's any translation issue, because the first thing I said is that you corrected Mr. Misetic when he used the word "order," and you said it is a letter. Now, what is -- were those who were addressees of this letter or instructions, were they duty-bound to follow that, or could they just say, Well, we try to do it in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were no proper conditions to implement what is stated there, then they did not act in accordance with this letter, but they had to inform the judge that they were unable to follow these instructions so that measures could be taken so that these prisoners could be taken elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the proper conditions were there, were the addressees under an obligation to follow the instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely the judge wrote this after the consultation with competent persons first in the Zadar Prison and then with competent persons in, as you can see, Zadar-Knin Police Administration, which means to say that an agreement had already been reached, because for every action taken, there must be a written trace in the file. So this is why the judge did this, so that somebody later on wouldn't say, Well, why were these people transferred here and not there, and so on. So there needed to be some written trace so that these proceedings could be continued on as soon as possible. As you can see, there were already decisions issued on putting these people into detention, and there were warrants issued. And based on the instruction of this judge and with the acquiescence of the Zadar-Split Police Administration, these people were taken to Zadar. We had similar situations previously, where after certain operations we had a large number of prisoners, so that the prisoner -- so that the prisons, in addition to the regular inmates and regular duties that they had, they could not take in this additional large number of people. And since all of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're spending a lot of time on what practically could oppose and whether it was good to do it this way. My question was a different one. My question was: that this is a letter sent by the Split Military Court, telling the Zadar-Knin Please Administration what to do with their prisoners, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could maybe -- I have a document that might clear this all up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait and see, but I notice that the answers of the witness were not very much focused on my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge, let's take this step by step. Now, the persons who are in custody, in the custody of the MUP at that moment, who actually has filed the criminal charges? In other words, which court had filed the criminal charges for acts against the Republic of Croatia, the military court or the civilian court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Military prosecutor. These were the crimes that I described earlier from Chapter 20 of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So in this situation, persons for whom an indictment had been filed by the military prosecutor for crimes against Croatia may have been held by the MUP; correct? And the judge is instructing what to do with people who are under his jurisdiction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: They could be under the jurisdiction of the MUP, but the law specifies clearly for how long, for what period of time. At that time, I think the dead-line was 48 hours. We need to look at the specific provision of the Law on Criminal Procedure, as to the exact period of time within which, following their arrest, they had to be taken to the investigating judge for further proceedings and questioning. That is to say that back in those days as well as now, the MUP was not competent to decide on its own how long they could keep somebody in custody. There were very specific provisions regarding that. As for this letter or memo, I can't see here -- or, rather, I can only see that there is a decision on putting these people in detention and that there was also a warrant, and most likely after this there followed an investigation and, later on, an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document on this topic. 65 ter 5277, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by the last answer. You said, As for this letter, I can only see that there is a decision putting these people in detention, and there was also a warrant, and most likely after this, there followed an investigation and, later on, an indictment. Could we have the document on our screen again. The previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the document. I have understood your question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Because the document starts that: "We inform you that all of the accused against whom criminal charges were filed for ..." Does this mean that -- you said criminal charges were filed. Is that something different from being indicted? The language, at least in English, is again "accused," and often the distinction is made between suspected persons and accused persons. It further reads criminal charges were filed for criminal offences. Therefore, that if I want to reconcile that an investigation first had to follow, I do not fully understand, perhaps, why the terminology "accused" against whom criminal charges were filed, how I have to understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back now and explain to you some terms from the Croatian Law on Criminal Procedure, and this may clarify the issue for you. In the Law on Criminal Procedure, we have a term "suspect," which is a person who is suspected of having committed a crime. And then there is a term "accused" and "indictee." And then after the -- at the end of this provision, it is stated that an accused is any person -- is -- comes under a law where that person is suspected of having committed a crime. "Indictee" is a person against whom an indictment was issued, and that indictment is final. "Accused" can also be a person against whom an indictment was issued, but maybe that indictment is not final yet. I cannot comment on this letter by my colleague, but in this case I believe that these were the accused against whom an indictment was issued. But as you can see in further text, that indictment is not final yet because there is a decision on placing them in detention, and there is also a warrant issued. Detention can also be given in the pre-trial proceedings, in the preliminary proceedings, but then perhaps that person is not available to the courts. In this particular case -- I need to see the list, but perhaps that is not vital. Among those persons, there were also the prisoners, and perhaps they were placed under investigation, but they were unavailable at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, that you say that although your initial answer was that only after an investigation, later on an indictment would be issued, that you do not exclude for the possibility, on the basis of the terminology used, this would cover also persons already indicted, but perhaps the indictment not having taken yet its final form, and that they might still have been at large. Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm advised that the number I -- the next document that I called up is exhibit -- should be Exhibit P909.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from the Ministry of the Interior, dated 21 August 1995, situation and treatment of -- it a final -- sorry, the subject is: "Final report on the treatment of prisoners of war in the reception centre for prisoners of war." And before I turn the page, did the International Committee of the Red Cross have access to persons -- prisoners of war, as far as you know, including persons who were held under the jurisdiction of the Military Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: We had regular visits of the representatives of the Red Cross, I mean their main committee in Geneva, who regularly came to visit all prisoners of war under the jurisdiction of the Military Court in Split and were placed in all prisons, in Sibenik, Zadar, and Dubrovnik. These persons that they visited, among other things, also were entitled to write a letter on a form supplied by them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just ask you an additional question. Did the Red Cross ever express any concerns about the treatment of prisoners held under the jurisdiction of the Split Military Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I know that we, pursuant to their request, whenever they would come to thank us for enabling them to make a visit, would show these letters written to their relatives. We did not want to read these letters because we thought it was a private matter of everybody who wrote them, but occasionally we would look at some of the letters written by these prisoners, and even they never complained in those letters about any mistreatment, be it at the time of their arrest or while they were in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention to paragraph 1.5, which is page 2 in the English, and I believe it should be the next page in Croatian. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, still the previous answer is a bit of a puzzle for me. Who would show the letters that apparently prisoners sent to their relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Representatives of the Red Cross, who would come to make visits. They would inform the Court about what they had done. They would inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have copies of the letters sent by the prisoners? No. You said: "If, pursuant to their request, whenever they would come to thank us for enabling them to make a visit, would show these letters written to their relatives," which I understand, and that's what you confirm, that the Red Cross would show the letters, which you said you didn't wish to read, but now and then you did. But occasionally, you said: "... we would look at some of the letters written by these prisoners, and even they never complained in those letters about any mistreatment," which suggests that you had read them at least occasionally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that even nowadays, nowadays, when it comes to prisoners writing letters to their relatives or anybody else, the Court is duty-bound to read those letters before they assent, because it is forbidden to write in the letters something about the course of proceedings, or offend the Court, or anything of that nature. That was the reason why the Red Cross would give us this letter, and in cases of persons who were tried for some of the grave offences against the Republic of Croatia, we would look at those letters to see whether that person made a comment about the work of courts, whether they wrote in that letter something that they shouldn't have written there. That was the only reason. And as I said, it is done even nowadays to make sure that there is nothing in those letters that are forbidden. I apologise. No copies of those letters were ever kept at the court in files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try now to understand your testimony. Whereas you initially said that you didn't wish to read those letters and that you only occasionally would look at some of them, this was -- which I'm not criticising in any way. This was the ordinary control of a correspondence of prisons which we find. Then I asked you whether you read them, and you more or less said the Red Cross would give those letters and you would look at them. Now, this all in answer to whether the Red Cross ever complained about the treatment, because that was the question that was put to you by Mr. Misetic, whether the Red Cross had any problems. Your answer entirely focuses on what you found in the letters as what the prisoners, knowing that there would be a kind of, I would say, normal censorship in detention situations, that you would read them. But whether the Red Cross ever complained or had any comments, that question has not been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I emphasised that, in the beginning, that we never had any complaint from any prisoner. I also have to point out that in these letters, if they did not want to write something to somebody, they could write a sort of a complaint, and I had never seen it. So there were never any complaints, be it verbal ones from the Red Cross or in those letters, because the Red Cross would have been duty-bound to inform us of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer started by saying that there were never any concerns expressed by the Red Cross, so that these were the two first words, "no, never," and then you explained this by referring exclusively to the letters you had seen and that were given to you by the Red Cross. But I do understand that the Red Cross, itself, apart from what was found in the letters, never expressed any concern. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was never any concern expressed, be it by the Red Cross or in the letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Mr. Misetic, I am looking at the clock. I don't know what -- first of all, I do not know how much time you need. Second, I do not know whether this is a suitable moment or whether that would come soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have maybe 15 minutes left, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is too much. Would this be a suitable moment or would you like --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, we'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Matulovic, I showed you paragraph 1.5. Does that -- there were some dates mentioned as to visits to the Split -- sorry, to the -- visits to the prisoners of war by the Red Cross from Geneva occurred four times, on the 7th, 10th, 11th, and 19th of August. Does that -- is that consistent with your recollection as to how frequently members of the ICRC from Geneva visited detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember now how frequent these visits were, but I wish to emphasise that the dates referred to, August 1995, when there were frequent visits, but they used to visit them frequently even before the Operation Storm. It wasn't as frequent as this, but it was regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to paragraphs -- starting at paragraph 2.3, which is page 3 in the English and page 3 in Croatian. Now, we see -- we start to see paragraphs that refer to how many -- of the total number of prisoners of war in the MUP Reception Centre, how many were brought to the investigative judge at the Military Court in Split. So, for example, in paragraph 2.3, it says: "Out of a total number of 183 brought to the Reception Centre, 81 prisoners, against whom criminal reports had been filed, were brought before the investigating judge at the Military Court in Split. "Out of the total number of prisoners brought before the military investigating judge, criminal reports were filed against 72 prisoners because of reasonable grounds to suspect that they had committed a crime described and sanctioned under Article 1 of the Law on Crimes of Subversive and Terrorist Activities against the state sovereignty ..." And then if we go through the document, there are various other references to prisoners of war held by the MUP being transferred to the military courts. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why those prisoners were transferred from the MUP to the Military Court? Actually, let me just show you one more portion of this document, page 6 in the English, which is paragraph 4.1. And they had put together a table which indicated, for example, the first entry, that Pupovac, Rade, was transferred to the Military Court on the 9th of August, 1995. Can you explain to the Court why such individuals were being transferred from the jurisdiction -- or transferred from the custody of MUP and into the custody of the Military Court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I already answered this question during my earlier testimony, when I said that there were dead-lines strictly set out in the Law on Criminal Procedure by which the suspects had to be further prosecuted. And in order to keep to the dead-lines, in the pre-trial proceedings they would be brought before the investigative judge for further procedure. And as for the number which I cannot see on the screen now, that was 183 and 81, that's the usual practice to this day, and it's in accordance with the provisions of the Law on Procedure, that if, in the pre-trial proceedings, facts are not established that would serve as grounds for suspicion or reasonable suspicion, then this person is not further prosecuted, and probably this is why the number of persons who were brought before a court was reduced to such an extent and others were released. As for the criminal offences, I mentioned during my earlier testimony, also, if you have a closer look at these articles, these are specifically the crimes which fall within the jurisdiction of the Military Court. That's the violation of territorial integrity, subversive activities, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a different topic, which is the issue of the Serb persons in the UN camp in Knin. First, can you tell the Court what role you had, if any, in the issue of the detainees in the Knin camp? I shouldn't say -- the persons who were in the Knin camp in August and September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: As for the persons who came, as far as I remember, to this Reception Centre South, they were prisoners of war, and among them there were also civilians who were refugees and who simply found shelter there. We got this information, and I must say that we set up, I couldn't call it a commission, but a group that included policemen, members of intelligence services, military services, and also the Military Court, and also the County Court in Split. What was the reason to form this group? The reason was what we talked about earlier. We saw the memo or the instructions, and the fact was that among the civilians in this camp -- it's a stupid to call it a camp; it was a reception centre. There were some people there that we had already launched criminal proceedings against, and there was a great danger that these persons, together with civilians who were not prosecuted in any way whatsoever, that once they were released and they were on their way out of Croatia, they were to be exchanged, they would be unavailable for the Croatian judiciary, and therefore we had a list of these persons. We had a list with first and last names, as you can see on this table, and the only goal of the persons from the judiciary was that such persons, if they were there among the civilians, should be singled out, should be separated, for further prosecution before Croatian courts, whether military ones or county courts, if a person was accused of war crimes. I have to say that the meeting was also attended by a high-ranking UNPROFOR official. I think that he was French, and he requested that for each such persons that we were looking for at this reception centre, he wanted to see the original file that existed in courts in connection with the criminal proceedings conducted against these persons, and we provided this. I have to emphasise that in a certain way, we also considered the pressure that we might be under if any of the prosecuted persons, especially for serious crimes such as war crimes, might be released from the reception centre, that then later on Croatian citizens would complain and say that we had let war criminals slip through and that they had run away and they had committed crimes in Croatia, and that we were dealing with other things. And we wouldn't even let them think something like that, and let alone let it happen. That was our main goal when we attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could, Madam Registrar, call up 65 ter 2441, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Judge Matulovic, this is a memo written by --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I haven't it, no page currently. Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a written -- a memo written by Mr. Husein Al-Alfi who's reporting on a meeting that you had with a Mr. Zhang, Z-h-a-n-g, on the 20th or 21st of September, 1995. Do you recall, first of all, having such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the memo purports to record some of the conversation that allegedly took place, and I wanted to just ask you a question about paragraph 2. It states -- if we could turn the page in English, please, as well. Now, it says, first of all, concerning the 38 persons who were in the Sector South camp and who were suspected, that: "The military court in Split is only handling one case of the 38, that is, the case of Djuric, Zdravko." Can you tell the Court why the Military Court would have been handling only one of the 38 cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to answer your previous question. After Storm, I had many meetings with representatives of various organisations, governmental, non-governmental, so simply I cannot remember all of them. Now that I see what you are showing me on the screen, this gentleman was probably there and we must have had a conversation. I don't think it's an invented document. I don't see the heading here. I think this was at some point in September 1995 or later. It's possible that even before this date, there was some sort of exchange or amnesty and that this person, Zdravko Djuric, was then prosecuted again after that. I cannot remember exactly, but in any case he was under the jurisdiction of the Military Court, which means that there was a crime from Chapter 20 or the Article 1 of the Law on Subversive Activities. Just a second, please, if you can bear with me. Here, in item 3, I mention that this case would be prosecuted, but not before October 1995, so it means that it was probably a case that we received later or -- I don't know. I cannot really remember the details at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, do you know what the other 37 may have been charged with?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: They were certainly all accused of crimes that were under the jurisdiction of the Military Court. It could have been war crimes, and if there were any such accused, then the cases were transferred to the County Court for further procedure. And if the cases were under our jurisdiction, then they would be dealt with by the Military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you about the second sentence in paragraph 2. It says: "Judge Matulovic confirmed that all the accused would be detained in civilian prisons, since military prisons were only for HV soldiers." Is it correct that military prisons were only for HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where would --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Military prisons were used for HV soldiers if these soldiers were sentenced for violations of discipline, and you could go there for two months for violations of discipline. As far as I can remember, that's where they served their sentences. Not a single civilian - let me call them civilians - who were under the jurisdiction of military courts after being arrested and brought before an investigating judge, could not be sent to a civilian prison, so they were not held there - the military prisons, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the prisoners of war from the RSK Army; in other words, military persons from the army of the so-called ARSK. Where would they be held, in military or civilian prisons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: For us, for the military judiciary, there were no military prisons. They were exclusively detainees in civilian prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 2441 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1623, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Mr. President. Judge Matulovic, thank you for answering my questions. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Cermak Defence, any need to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have any question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic for the Markac Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will have a couple of questions that would last maybe 15 minutes or 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Matulovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will ask you several questions, and I kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your knowledge and recollection. When we talk about military courts, where were they located, physically?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The military courts were physically located, according to the decree, at the seats of the district courts which are now the county courts. So the Military Court in Split was located in the building of the District Court. The Military Court -- the detached department in Zadar was also in the building of the District Court. It was the same in Sibenik. They were always in the buildings of the district courts -- civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You explained to us how the judges of military courts were appointed from civilian courts. What about the personnel, the recording clerks and the administrative personnel in military courts; were they military personnel or civilian personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: They were all civilian personnel because, as I said, the military courts were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, and there was no way for any employees of courts, except for the judges that we talked about already, I mean all the administrative staff, the court-recording clerks, could be military personnel. They were our personnel there, still some of them, in courts. Some worked there and then left later on, but they were all employees of civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As for the salaries for administrative personnel, who paid the salaries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The Justice Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the regulations in according to which the judges acted, whether they were substantive or procedural, what regulations were these?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I said at the beginning there were two decrees. One related to the organisation of the judicial authorities, and the other one was a decree on the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure in the case of imminent threat of war, et cetera. Let me not quote the entire title. This decree also included the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was then applied both in military and civilian courts, and this decree reduced the Law on Criminal Procedure to certain specific chapters. For example, what was reduced was a chapter of objection to the indictment. That's a procedural statute which existed before, and it still exists. At that time, the application of this chapter of the Law on Criminal Procedure was reduced, and I think this was the major reduction that we had, so that we could conduct the proceedings as quickly as possible. We all know from experience, all of us working in the judiciary, that whether an indictment will come into force or not depends on many factors, and sometimes a long period might relapse [as interpreted] between an indictment is issued and when it is applied. And, excuse me, as for the substantive law, it was always the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you started your next question already when the interpreters were still busy interpreting the previous answer of the witness. Could you make a small pause between question and answer, and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Matulovic, we could say that there was no, under quotations, "military law" according to which the military courts in the Republic of Croatia acted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: There was no military law, nor the military judiciary, which is even more important. This was all civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the martial law, the notion of martial law?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there ever such courts in Croatia, the martial law courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Whether they existed, I don't know about the distant past in Croatia, but since I have been working in the judiciary, I never heard of any form of proceedings that would have any elements of martial court proceedings, let alone that there could exist such institutions as martial courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... accuracy of the transcript in page 45, line 12. I think it's a wrong translation of the [B/C/S spoken]. It reads here "martial law." I was talking about court-martial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, Mr. Mikulicic, you can ask to be verified, but to replace the given translation by another one, although, as a matter of fact, from the answer it's clear that that is what you asked the witness about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to be on the safe side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any dispute about this or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, you introduce whether something exists, when no one has ever suggested it does exist, and then we get the confirmation that it doesn't exist. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just interpreting my question, Your Honour, because I was asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, I mean, the whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Matulovic, you talked about the procedure that was used in military courts and also civilian courts, and that it had its stages. According to your experience, from the moment when you learn that a crime has been committed to the moment when possibly a judgement could be issued against the perpetrators, what was the period of time that we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I did not exactly understand your question. Which period do you have in mind? Do you mean how long would it last, or -- how long would it last? There were the stages of the proceedings that I talked about earlier. There's the pre-trial proceedings; that's what the police is in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a second. [In English] [Previous translation continues]... refers to the transcript which was already done before. When the witness is talking about "predkazneni postupak," which is a Croatian term, that term has been translated as a pre-trial proceedings, which is, from my point of view, it's not accurate translation, because "pre-trial proceedings" implies that the proceedings has been held before the court, which is not true. Pre-criminal proceedings is something that has been held apart from the courts, within the police jurisdiction, let me put it this way. You will remember, Your Honour, that we have already such kind of, let me say, wrong translation earlier, and that we agreed -- my learned colleague also agreed with me that this term "predkazneni postupak" in Croatian should be properly translated as "pre-criminal proceedings," not the "pre-trial proceedings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether -- I appreciate that you come to an agreement on how it should be understood. Now, one of the problems of translations in legal matters is that the legal concepts in the one system do not always correspond with the legal concepts in the other, so where you rightly seek an agreement with the Prosecution on how to understand these terms and what they actually mean, that's appreciated. Whether these are wrong translations or whether these are second-best, where there's no first-best translation, seems to be more likely to me, because "pre-criminal proceedings" could -- well, I'm not a native English speaker, but that could create a bit of confusion as well, what means "pre-criminal"? Is that before the crime was committed or before criminal proceedings? No, I'm just pointing out to you that whether the translation is right or wrong is not easy to establish.
