And I'm very hesitant to do that, but it's always clear that we clarify what is meant by a witness or by you when using a certain legal concept or legal term which is used in the systems in the former Yugoslavia, and especially in Croatia. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could clarify that topic in a couple of minutes with the witness so that it could be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I use a rough term, "wrong translation." Probably it is not a proper word for it. It's simply, as you put it, the difference between two legal systems, which is sometimes very hard to translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm confident that in view of the explanation you gave, why you considered that wrong translation, that the interpreters would have understood there's not to be any criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Matulovic, for those of us who come from the Croatian judiciary, we know the distinction, but given that the procedure before this Court and also in the common-law system is somewhat different, I would ask you to describe, in a couple of sentences, what does it mean, "preliminary criminal proceedings," and who conducts it in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to answering this question, I would like to mention something because I have been coming across such minor problems since the time when I worked in the Military Court and also when I was an investigating judge; namely, I always insisted that exactly what I say be translated accurately, because every word has its weight. I'm not saying that it's easy to translate every term from our Law on Criminal Procedure, but everything needs to be done as accurately as possible. And based on what I have heard, the interpreters here are doing their job well, but it is quite understandable that they have difficulty with some terms. Now, why did I say all of this? I've been a judge for 33 years. I went to all kinds of courts, and it is quite clear to me how a wrong application of legislative terminology can be quite damaging. And this is what I expected here when it comes to preliminary criminal proceedings. These are the proceedings conducted by the police. I have to say that I think in Article 6 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, it is stipulated when criminal proceedings actually begin. There is a huge difference there. Criminal proceedings are instituted based on the request of the authorised public prosecutor. Once a public prosecutor files a request, be it an investigative request or a draft indictment, this is when criminal proceedings are launched, and they are ongoing all -- for a long time, until the prosecutor is acting. In the investigative proceedings, the proceedings are launched once a request to launch investigation is filed, and it goes on either until an indictment is issued or until the prosecutor decides to drop charges. I think that I have now clarified the stages and the proceedings now so that it's easier for everybody now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I will now go back to my initial question on how long the proceedings lasted. How long did they last for certain crimes? Give me a rough estimate. Was it a month, or two, or a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Even though you said "a rough estimate," it's quite difficult to give a rough estimate, and that's because we have, say, proceedings for a less serious crime, where we have eight accused, and then we can have proceedings for a grave crime, where we only have one accused. So the duration of proceedings, criminal proceedings, depend on many factors -- depends on many factors. It depends on the number of accused, on all the steps that need to be taken. So it is difficult to give even a rough estimate. But at any rate, these proceedings were accelerated as much as possible at the time, and this is why there was this provision on the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure so that there would be legislative grounds for speeding these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Let us turn to another topic briefly. Once the criminal proceedings were instituted, in your statement, in paragraph 17, you said that once there was a final judgement the Ministry of Justice would be informed by the courts so that they could do their activities in order to establish the status of the accused. My question is: Did they inform the competent military bodies about the fact that criminal proceedings were launched, that there was a decision to launch an investigation, or that there was a decision to issue an indictment? Were they informed then, or were they only informed once there was a final judgement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: That was a duty of the courts based on the law. The Ministry of Justice, the Personnel Administration, had to be informed, as well as the command of the relevant unit, about the fact that a Croatian soldier was detained by an investigating judge, because they at all times had to be informed about the whereabouts of the soldier who had been arrested. Once a judgement was issued finding a Croatian soldier guilty of a crime and sentencing him, once again the court was duty-bound to send one copy of the judgement to the Ministry of Justice, to the Personnel Administration, because they, based on the current legislation, had to make a decision on what to do with that soldier following his conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I see you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could check the witness's answer as to the Ministry involved at line 7 and at line 13, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What ministry did you intend to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that later, when you said that the court was duty-bound to send one copy of the judgement to ... did you then also want to refer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Minister of defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the answer, when reference was made to the Ministry of Justice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I apologise. Just a second, please. [In English] "... to send one copy of the judgment to the Ministry of Justice." No, Ministry of Defence in here also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In both instances where the witness referred to the Ministry of Justice, he intended to refer to the Ministry of Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, the same question now in relation to the numbers of the Ministry of the Interior. What was the duty of the courts if a member of the Ministry of Interior was detained or if a judgement was issued against them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The duty was identical, except that the information was sent to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers, Mr. Matulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Matulovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Matulovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, you were asked as to when a military court would have jurisdiction on a particular case, and your response was, and this is at page 10, line 8: "When it was established that the crime was committed by a serviceman." Now, if crimes were committed in an area which was under the control of the military, would it not be the responsibility of the military police to investigate that crime to ascertain if, in fact, members of the HV were involved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I have already stated that the territorial jurisdiction was defined as the jurisdiction of the Military Court in Split, and it also specified areas of which courts came under that. In the areas of some courts, there were more activities, and in areas of some other courts, there were fewer. Now, if there was army in that territory and a soldier committed a crime from the jurisdiction of military courts, then naturally it was the military police and the military prosecutor, and later the military courts that were involved. However, I have to emphasise, and I'll give you a very specific example. A town that came under the jurisdiction of the Military Court in Split, in that town they found a body of an old woman who had been killed, and that immediately gave rise to the notion that this was a crime against a civilian. Regardless of the fact that this came under the territorial jurisdiction of the Military Court, the case was immediately taken over by civilian police, civilian prosecutor, civilian investigating judge, because you have probably already heard that the war crimes did not fall under the jurisdiction of military courts. Therefore, in order to establish what was the -- to determine subject-matter jurisdiction, it wasn't really important to establish whether the area was under military control or not, but rather it was important to establish what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, following that, and in fact you also mention this in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to understand the testimony, your question. Ms. Mahindaratne, your question was about, How could you assert that an HV member would be the perpetrator? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness gave a clear answer on another aspect of jurisdiction; that is, how could you ascertain whether it was a war crime or not, because you were referring to one rule of jurisdiction, which is that, apart from war crimes, that HV members, having committed or sufficiently reasons to believe that the perpetrators of a crime were HV members, triggered jurisdiction. And the witness gave, I take it, a perfectly right answer, but on a different question; that is, whether the exclusion for war crimes would apply and how to establish that. I do not mind if you want to put one question and then he'll answer to another --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to ask him to clarify, because I was going to take him from there to the point I want to take him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you'd allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll allow you to continue, but I just wanted to express my concern about questions and answer being about the same subject. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Matulovic, your testimony is that war crimes were not within the jurisdiction of the military courts. Now, isn't it correct that the underlying crime which could be the subject of a war crime prosecution could be charged as an ordinary crime in the military courts? For example, if it related to a case of a killing incident, the perpetrator could be charged under Article 34 of the Criminal Code in the military court; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you have put quite a confusing and imprecise question to me. I will try to give you an answer. A war crime is one thing. It can be committed even without committing a murder. A murder is a crime against life and limb. That's its definition. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, my point is the underlying crime which could be the subject of a war crime prosecution, such as with a killing or any other incident, could be charged as an ordinary crime under your Criminal Code in the military courts. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: If it is established right away that this was a case of murder, which is quite difficult in the beginning, and that's why I gave you that example about an old lady being killed in the area where there was combat, and that immediately gave rise to the idea that this could have been a case of a war crime because it involved a civilian. Now, whether it was a murder or not will be established later during the investigation. And it could be argued that it wasn't a war crime but, rather, an ordinary murder. And if it was an ordinary murder and if it was committed by a Croatian Army -- by a Croatian soldier, then he would be tried before the Military Court, as there were many cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Similarly, for example, in the case of destruction of property or arson, that could be tried as an ordinary crime in the military courts, is that correct, if the perpetrator was a member of the HV?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I have said so already. All crimes which could be committed by civilians, in cases where they were committed by soldiers, unless they were war crimes, were tried before the Military Court, unless those people ceased being military servicemen before the indictment was issued and the proceedings were launched. We've already discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is a bit of confusion about what you want to hear from the witness, and either the witness doesn't understand fully or you're not precise enough. Let me try to see whether I can -- first of all, whether I understand what you wanted to know and, secondly, to hear whether -- what the answer would be by Mr. Matulovic. Mr. Matulovic, someone is killed - it is a civilian - under circumstances which give quite some reasons to believe that it may well have been a war crime. Now, in phrasing the charges against a person, you could leave out the specific elements for murder as a war crime and just indict that person for murder, irrespective of whether these elements which would make it a war crime could be proven, yes or no. Was it within the discretion of the military prosecutor to -- well, let's say to limit the charges to an ordinary murder, which would trigger the jurisdiction of the Military Court? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the question you had on your mind, Ms. Mahindaratne? Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you came precisely to what I said in the beginning, that the question was quite confusing and it contained several elements. Military prosecutor is the person who directs the proceedings and conducts them, in cooperation with the judge, both during the investigation phase, during the indictment phase, and during the trial phase. That is precisely the clarification of what I said; namely, that the question had several elements and that I couldn't answer them precisely. So everything is a matter of assessment based on the facts, assessment by the military prosecutor. And he could have worked together with a civilian colleague, and they could have said, Well, take a look at this case and let's discuss and let's decide what we're going to do. It's up to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, for the -- now, your testimony is it's the military prosecutor's jurisdiction or the Military Court's jurisdiction is triggered at the point when the perpetrator's status is established as a member of the HV. Now, my first question to you was: In an area which is under military control, where there was, say, a significant amount of burning of a property, is it not the responsibility of the military police to investigate into the matter to establish --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: No leading questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any objection against leading, it will come from the other party. And I do understand that you may mix up your professional duties with your position as a witness. Leading questions are not, under all circumstances, objected to, and it's for the Court to decide to what extent it will allow leading questions. Now, I took it that it was rather a hypothetical question than a leading question. Ms. Mahindaratne knows this Court is not very fond of hypothetical questions, but you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it the responsibility of the military police, in fact, to investigate crimes committed in an area which is under the control of the military to establish if, in fact, the -- if, in fact, members of the HV were involved in the crime; not to establish, in fact, the status of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could give two answers to that question. The first is that the military police in the area which is under military control, as you phrase it, has to carry out some sort of police investigation as soon as something happens. Military police, and I emphasise once again, regardless of whether it is an area under military control or not, has to act if the suspect is a serviceman, without any doubt. In such areas which you call areas under military control, there could have been civilians who are guilty of arson, who set up a house on fire due to some revenge, that is, a blood-feud that is 50 years old. In those cases it will be the civilian police acting, and not the military police, even though that area is under military control, or the civilian police could be acting in cooperation with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was with regard to instances where the status of the suspect had not been established yet, but the crime has been committed in an area under military control. Isn't there a responsibility on of the part of the military police to investigate if, in fact, members of the HV were involved? That is the point. I'm not talking about where the status of the perpetrator has already been established as military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question as confusing because I think the first portion of the question is contradicted by the second portion of the question. The first portion of the question says: "In circumstances where the status of the suspect has not been established yet ..." And then she says: "I'm talking about where the status of the person has already been established as military."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to establish this status could mean two things. The first is: Who's the suspect? Is that, at face value, a military or civilian? And the second is whether somebody wearing a military uniform is really a military person. So it's a two-layer question. Let's try again, Ms. Mahindaratne, to see whether I understood what you wanted to ask from the witness. I'm going to sin against my own rules; that is, I put a hypothetical question to you. I see a significant military presence in a certain area where I see not many civilians left. I've heard about arson that had happened in those days. I'm a military police officer. I am at a distance of 300 metres from a house, and I see some people with jerry-cans, and suddenly the house is ablaze. What should I do? Should I go there and see whether the guys with jerry-cans are civilians, or should I say it has not been established that the ones who most likely have put the house at fire are military, and therefore I remain passive?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that more or less the situation you had in mind, Ms. Mahindaratne? Could you tell us what is this military policeman supposed to do - and he's not accompanied by a civilian police officer, because then the answer might more easy, but he's just on his own - should he go there and try to find out, or should he say, It has not been sufficiently established that this is a matter which falls within my competence to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have come to the questions that could have been perhaps better put to some of my predecessors here who testified about the competence of military police. But let me try to give you an answer to this question, even though I don't deal with police matters. If police observes directly an unlawful act, any policeman, including military policemen, should act and establish the identity of persons observed on the scene, and these are their competencies. If they establish that these persons with jerry-cans are civilians, they will act accordingly. If they establish that none of them are military personnel, then they will also act accordingly, and they will detain those persons there until civilian police arrives. And then once the civilian police arrives, they may act together with them in order to carry out certain on-site activities, ensure preservation of evidence, and so on. Now, I would like to say something to Madam Prosecutor. I want to clarify something. Military courts, should they learn that six persons committed a crime, and that out of those six, five were civilians and one was a serviceman, because of that one serviceman, their jurisdiction would be triggered and they would conduct the proceedings, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Matulovic, for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you referred to war crimes prosecutions being in the jurisdiction of the civilian courts or, should I say, the district or county/state courts. Are you aware of any war crimes prosecutions being conducted at the district or county/state courts against members of the HV for crimes committed in August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a document by Mr. Misetic. That was P2251. And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just -- Madam Registrar, if you could just bring it up. And you were asked -- in fact, that document is -- two other addresses are the commander of the Split Military District and the Split Garrison Command. And you were asked as to what the purpose of sending that documents to those addressees is. And your answer, this is at page 22, line 15. You say: "Both commanders must know if there are any infractions of discipline." And you go on to say: "I emphasise that the military disciplinary proceedings and also the criminal proceedings, if they followed from these reports, that anything needed to be conducted has nothing to do with the other." That's your response. Now, isn't it correct that a criminal offence conducted by a member of the HV is also considered as a major violation of military discipline under the Code of Military Discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in the daily reports, both the infractions of the provisions about military discipline were mentioned, specifically in this document a traffic accident is mentioned because of excess speed and so on. Let me emphasise again. The proceedings for violations of military discipline and for criminal offences are two different kinds of proceedings, which does not mean that if a serviceman, by his conduct, committed a crime, must not be charged with disciplinary measures, but if there is a disciplinary offence, then it cannot be treated in the same way as the criminal offence because they are covered by different laws. It could happen that a certain military personnel might commit an offence, but, that at the same time, it is not a breach of discipline. But in any case, the proceedings are separate, so they do not entail -- one doesn't entail the other and how these proceedings would be further conducted. And here specifically in this document, you can see that because of conditions on the road and because of speed, there was a traffic accident. He hit a pedestrian and so on. She was crossing at a zebra crossing, and it's a typical traffic accident. There was serious injury. Now, whether the commander, depending on this factual description, would also find here elements of breach of discipline, that's the matter of the commander's assessment. He could do that, but he doesn't have to do it. And the military prosecutor would then continue the proceedings, and then this would be transferred to the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that under the Code of Military Discipline, a crime committed by a member of the HV, such as a case of killing, or destruction or burning of property, or theft, would be considered as a major violation of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Now we are talking about disciplinary responsibility and disciplinary proceedings. I can answer this as well, and I believe that this will be clear, how this was done when, in 1997, I came to the Disciplinary Military Court in Split. Maybe there could be some difficulties with understanding, but I'll try to be as precise as I can. In the list of disciplinary offences -- there are disciplinary offences, not just disciplinary infractions which are less serious violations of military discipline, and disciplinary offences are more serious forms of violation of military discipline, it was prescribed that the disciplinary offence, if an active serviceman -- if there were reasonable grounds to suspect that an active serviceman committed an offence for which proceedings are launched and then conducted, because the institutions are duty-bound to do that, it's done ex officio, these are traffic accidents and other such offences. The reasonable grounds exist when the decision to launch an investigation is issued or when an indictment is issued. And the person who is -- the indictment for this offence does not include the description of the offence, as the indictment or the decision to conduct an investigation will include it, with all the elements and details of the commission of the crime, but it says that such and such a person, with or without a rank, damaged the honour and the reputation of the Croatian Army because an indictment was issued before the County Court in Split because of the offence of drug abuse. So, for example, because of the fact that an indictment was issued, regardless of what the judgement might be, the person was disciplinarily responsible, and the procedure then, if it was drug abuse, would be continued before a regular court in accordance with the indictment that was issued. So I hope that I managed to draw this distinction between disciplinary responsibility and criminal responsibility. You saw the example which I mentioned, where the factual description from the indictment does not necessarily include disciplinary proceedings that would be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe you didn't quite answer my question, Mr. Matulovic. My question was: If an incident of murder or destruction or burning of property, or theft, committed by a member of the HV would be considered as a serious form of violation of military discipline. Is it a "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just establish a date. I think it's important to establish what time-frame Ms. Mahindaratne is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Particularly those committed in August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I already -- as for the disciplinary proceedings before 1995, I cannot talk about this because I wasn't working on this. There were special disciplinary courts or whatever they were called. But I'm telling you, in principle, by using this example, if it was serious, because you keep talking about serious crimes such as arson or murder - there were less serious crimes - then in any case conditions would be met to conduct disciplinary proceedings because of damage done to the reputation of the military forces. And I think that I couldn't give a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you - I think have you your statement there, Mr. Matulovic - to page 7 of your statement, and I'm referring to paragraph 2 there. That is the paragraph just above the question numbered 6. You refer to investigations. You say: "From the aforementioned, the following has to be pointed out. The investigation is not conducted by the police. Investigation, in terms of the Croatian judiciary system, is a court procedure conducted by the court. For criminal offences that fall under the jurisdiction of regular courts, the investigation is conducted by the investigative judge of the County Court. For criminal offences that fall under the jurisdiction of the military judiciary, the investigation is conducted by the investigating judge of the Military Court." Now, in order for an investigative judge to conduct an investigation, be it the military court or the civilian court, the judge should receive a report of the crime; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: But you left something out a little bit here, certain details that would lead me to an appropriate answer. Firstly, it is noted here that the investigation is not conducted by the police. If you remember the answer to the questions asked by Mr. Mikulicic, I emphasised that one of the stages of the criminal procedure is the preliminary criminal proceedings in which police is the one who carries it out. It's the preliminary criminal proceedings before an investigation. If a judge is to continue conducting an investigation, he does not need to receive reports in order to continue conducting an investigation, regardless of whether it's a military or civilian investigative judge, he has to have, and I noted that in the answer to Mr. Mikulicic, he has to have the request for investigation from the prosecutor's office which is in charge of this. So it could be the municipal or the county/state attorney, or prosecutor's office. I believe this is an answer to your question. Let me repeat these are the stages of the procedure, and in the Law on Criminal Procedure, which I also already mentioned, there is an article which precisely provides when the criminal procedure begins. And my answer was and still is that a criminal procedure does not begin after a report that the judge may receive, but on a request of the prosecutor who is competent exclusively on that request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct, in order for the prosecutor to act and make that request of an investigative judge, the police or the military police, as the case may be, have to submit a report informing him that a crime has been committed and giving the specific location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Not only that, but in order for the investigative judge to take any further action, at the beginning the location might not be important, but all the other elements are important, the elements which are established in the preliminary criminal proceedings by the police and on the basis of which the military prosecutor, when we had military courts - now it would be a civilian prosecutor - would tell the police what to do next so that he could more successfully submit an investigation request to the investigative judge and launch the investigative procedure. So it is exclusively the responsibility of the military, or now, a civilian prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Matulovic, isn't it correct that during the period August and September 1995, there was a high number of crimes committed in the area known as the former Sector South, which was an area which came within your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I think that a question cannot include a hypothesis that a great number of criminal offences were perpetrated. What was the number of the criminal offences perpetrated, no one can know until the proceedings begin. And then there is the justified question: In all these areas, there were also civilians, and couldn't it happen -- now I am going to ask a hypothetical question, if you allow me - that someone who is leaving the area, as we said, out of spite, said, If I cannot use my house, no one's going to use it, and then he might set it on fire, and he's not a Croatian soldier or a Croatian citizen, he's leaving and then destroys something that he made so that no one else would be using it. And so the number of -- the great number of criminal offences, I think this is too extensive a term.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mr. Matulovic, Ms. Mahindaratne defined a period, asked you whether there were a high number of crimes committed in the area known as former Sector South, so there she gives a geographical invitation, and then she added "which was an area which came within your jurisdiction." She apparently was alluding to the geographical limits of the jurisdiction, although this might be easily misunderstood as to refer to the jurisdiction "ratione personae," it is what kind of persons came within a jurisdiction. So the last portion of the question is perhaps a bit problematic. Now, you very much, in your answer, focused on that last portion of the question. Ms. Mahindaratne, did you intend to seek further information when you said "Sector South, within your jurisdiction," to include the limits as far as the personal jurisdiction is concerned, or were you exclusively referring to crimes committed in this geographical area, in this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The latter, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you took a risk by referring to using the jurisdiction instead of saying "in the geographical area which was covered by your court." So --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just as a point of further clarification, and I don't think it's disputed by the parties, even the geographic area is not South Sector. So if we can be more precise, because there's a portion of Sector South -- a significant portion of Sector South which wouldn't have fallen geographically in this jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Matulovic, you understood the reference to jurisdiction as jurisdiction over HV members, whereas Ms. Mahindaratne wanted to ask you whether, then, the area in which you had jurisdiction, whether in that geographical area, which included major portions of Sector South, whether the number of crimes committed in August and September 1995 was high, which I understand to be relatively high compared to other periods of time. If you can answer the question, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I will answer that the notion of a great number is very relative. Three murders can be a huge number; and then six traffic accidents, a minor number, in the structure of offences committed. So we cannot talk generally about a great number of criminal offences. As many offences were committed, so many were prosecuted. And what is the number of offences that the Prosecutor is talking about, I don't know. I think it would be more interesting to ask such a question to someone from the Military Prosecutor's Office rather than me, because we would prosecute the cases that we would receive, the accused that we had. And I'm talking hypothetically. If there were ten murders committed in one area, though it wasn't the case, then it would be really a great number. But if there were four thefts where moto-cultivators were stolen, then it couldn't be compared with any number of offences. So this is why I said at the beginning that this is a hypothetical question. What's a great number of offences, and that the Presiding Judge also asked me about. It's a relative notion, because in certain crimes a great number cannot really be great; sometimes not. It depends, and it doesn't have to be related to the quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether this, or whether you could find somewhere within the next five minutes, a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could take the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me be more specific, Mr. Matulovic. Let me take an example, for instance, if you take Kistanje, which was an area which came within your area of jurisdiction, isn't it correct that in the period August and September, there were a high number of destruction and burnings in the municipality of Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to answer that you would have to have insight in all the cases and all the files of the Military Court, all the cases that were dealt with, also the cases at the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split, to say if there were really so many crimes, as you call them; how many crimes were prosecuted, whether these were really those crimes or it turned out later on that they were less serious. It's difficult now to answer this question on top of my head, especially about the area of Kistanje. At the Split Military Court area, we were responsible for the territory between Split and Zadar, so we had to cover too much territory to be able to say exactly what happened in Kistanje, whether it was 10, or 17, or 12 houses, whether there were thefts or burglaries in such and such a number. It's very difficult. One would need to have a look at the cases. You would have to ask the prosecutor to submit to you what was reported and then prosecute it in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry to interrupt again. A little transcript issue is still pending. I am referring to the territorial responsibility of the Split Military Court which has been mentioned in page 71, line 15 and 16 explicitly. I think that the witness has mentioned some other towns. Could we repeat the questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if we spent a lot of time on it, in view of the gist of the answer, do we need to clarify this at all? The gist of the answer being that we do not know because we don't have sufficient information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No, no, no, I'm referring to the responsibility for the territory which was under the Split Military Court, where the witness mentioned the town of Split and other town apart from Zadar. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's quicker to ask the witness. You mentioned the Split Military Court area as being between Split and Zadar and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sibenik and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, during 1995, after Operation Storm was completed, let's say from 7th August 1995 to end 1995, were you in any way informed that the military police, the 72nd Military Police Battalion specifically, had any difficulties in coping with their work in relation to investigation of crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: The part of the responsibilities of the military police was great. The scope of their responsibility was great. And as I said, there was also the huge territorial responsibility of the Military Court, and I don't know if the military police, with so many duties, would have any problems that would impede their work. And, after all, if they had it at that stage, they were duty-bound to inform the Military Police Administration and not us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think you answered my question. Mr. President, I think this is a good moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Matulovic, we'll have a break. I hope that the leading question is not any more bothering you, but you were educated in a non-common-law system; so was I. So apart from who objects and who decides, I meanwhile learned that leading questions are prohibited in examination-in-chief, but not that much in cross-examination. So we both learn every day. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, excuse me, Mr. President. This is an official. I can answer on this question. [Interpretation] The next time we see each other, but not here, but somewhere else, I will show you a certificate which I personally received from the Registrar of this Court after I completed the instruction to conduct proceedings according to the Anglo-Saxon system. And one of the lecturers was Mr. Kenneth Scott. I'm sure he is well known to my colleague and to everyone else. Let me not mention everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me say that then you are better off than me, because I have no such certificate, Mr. Matulovic. And I just wanted to -- I just wanted to give you some comfort for the break in relation to leading questions in examination-in-chief and cross-examination. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed. Could you give us any indication as to how much time you would approximately need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: About 20 minutes more, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, to questions from Mr. Misetic, and this is at page 26, line 15. You said that the prisons in Split were all crowded, and that was with prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: It was probably misinterpreted. I said should the prisons be over-crowded, that then the prisoners would be sent elsewhere. After such operations, we would normally have more prisoners than at other times. And not all of them were prisoners of war because the county and municipal courts had their proceedings in parallel, and their accused would share the same premises in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were shown a document by Mr. Misetic that was P909, which related to the number of prisoners of war that had been processed in your court. Let me also show you another document. And, Madam Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 7349, please. And this relates to a record of a meeting that the UNCRO Sector South members had with you on 8 January. It refers to -- and I'll just read this, refer a meeting of the 5th January -- my apologies, it says, 5th January, 1996, on the above subject: "Please find attached the list of 219 detainees released by Split Military Court. According to Judge Matulovic, president of the court, there would be no more trials by his court. I understand that the trials of those suspected of committing war crimes will be conducted by the Split County Court." Now, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber about approximately how many cases were processed by the Split Military Court against prisoners of war? An approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Very many, but I can't even give you a rough number. However I can confirm what is stated here, namely, that pursuant to an enactment of the president of the state, now late Dr. Franjo Tudjman, there was an amnesty, and they were all set free. And this sentence here, that there would be nor trials of war crimes suspects, meant that there were simply none anymore in the court. Following this document, we worked for another seven months, and we prosecuted other accused. There were a lot of them. And as for the prisoners of war, we had none of them after this amnesty. And this is just a message here in this document. And it says here: "I understand that the trials of those suspected of committing war crimes will be conducted by the Split County Court. And, yes, there were several such cases involving war crimes."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to at least give some idea as to what range of cases were tried against prisoners of war in the Split Military Court until the point of amnesty? Is it in the thousands or hundreds?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Not in thousands. It could be in hundreds. I'm now referring to the prisoners of war, and I'm emphasizing that this was exclusively the crimes from Chapter 20 of the Criminal Code. Several hundreds, yes, but I couldn't give you a more specific number. Let me tell you how this setting free looked like. We had 160 -- are you interested in this or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Matulovic, I don't have that much time, so I just wanted to get to the numbers. In addition to processes against prisoners of war, did the Split Military Court also file cases against members of the ARSK in absentia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing to try them for because the crimes against the Republic of Croatia -- this is what I wanted to tell you about, and then you told me that you had no time. Now, in those cases, if there was an amnesty, they issued a decision on suspending the proceedings, which automatically abolished any further detention. So regardless of what stage of the proceedings they were in, they were set free with involvement of the Red Cross or not, and they could go where they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, I don't intend to be rude, but my question was: In addition to these cases, were there, up until the point of amnesty, were there cases -- were there cases filed by the Military Court in Split in absentia against members of the RSK? I'm not talking about those in detention. I'm talking about those who were not in custody.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring exclusively to the Military Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to your court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears to state that there's a list that's supposed to be attached to the document, and I can't access it from e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There was no list in the document that was obtained by us, Mr. President. This is the only document that's available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the second question I have for counsel is if this was disclosed to us pursuant to 66(B).

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I then have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2596 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, I'm going to quickly show you a few documents and ask you a question. Madam Registrar, if I could have document 65 ter 7347, please. And if I could go -- if you could go to the next page, Madam Registrar. Mr. President, I should point out that the English -- in the English translation, the pages have been mixed up. Page 2 should be, in fact, page 3. So, Madam Registrar, if you could just move to page 3 on the English translation only. Mr. Matulovic, this is a case file, and you probably recognise, as we go through this in the Split Military Court, where you have been one of the members of the Bench which delivered the judgement, which was an acquittal, and the case concerns looting by three accused, two of whom were members of the HV. And, Madam Registrar, if you could move to -- if you could stay on that page. There we note -- it's recorded that amongst the records attached to this case file, there's a confirmation by battalion -- Sinj Military Police, 5th Company, dated 7th September, confirming that two of the accused, Stipe Krajina and Mladen Bandic were members of the Croatian military. And if you could move, Madam Registrar, to page 6, both English and -- I'm sorry, Croatian page 5. This is -- this is an official note of an interview of one of the accused, that is, Mladen Bandic. And if you could focus on paragraph 3 of the English translation. That's the last paragraph on the Croatian. It says -- it reads: "I," and that's the accused Mladen Bandic, "and the other accused went to Knin at 1630 today on 6th/9/1995 ..." And I won't take time reading the rest of the lines. Just six lines down, it reads: "I would like to emphasise that I am an expelled [Realtime transcript read in error "experienced"] person and had authorisation for the --" this is about removal of a tractor, "but did not take the authorisation with me because it was only valid for the day when it was issued, and I didn't use it on that day." Mr. President, there is a transcript error. I read -- this is at line 20. It reads: "I would like to emphasise that I am an expelled person," and it has been recorded as "experienced person."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could move, Madam Registrar, to English translation page 8, Croatian page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the second official note of interview by the second accused, and it reads: "At 06/09/1995, at 1630, Mladen Bandic" and the other accused, and they have arrived in this location. And if you move down six lines, it reads: "I was in the field last time when authorisations for cattle were being issued, but the next day they stopped being issued. Today I went to the municipality in Hrvace again to get [Realtime transcript read in error "give"] authorisation, but they told me that they weren't -- that there weren't any more cows at the collection centre, they had stopped issuing authorisations, and I should manage on my own." Now I want to show you a couple more documents. Mr. President, if this document could be tendered into evidence and given a mark. I just want to save time and show the witness several documents and ask a couple of questions, Mr. President; hence this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then wait until you've asked the questions, and then we can better assess the relevance and probative value of these documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it's not entirely clear to me yet, what probative interests these documents could serve. Meantime, if you've already called for the next document, then I'll give a correction to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 3919A [Realtime transcript read in error "3918A"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then page 79, line 15, where you said again "to give authorisation," it was to get authorisation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is a criminal report filed by the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, and you can note, Mr. Matulovic, at the top right-hand corner there is also the stamp of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office. Now, if we could move to, in the English, page 6; and in the Croatian, about two pages down. Madam Registrar, if you could move down. Okay, that's a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is again an official note of an accused charged of theft of cattle, and if you could focus on the last paragraph on the English translation. There is a paragraph going -- this is the paragraph which starts, Mr. Matulovic, "In order ..." "In order to be provided with nine cows, he was issued a receipt by the government commissioner for the Policnik area on 12 September 1995." And a few lines down, the last line: "They loaded nine calves there, at around 1730 hours, on the way back, they were stopped in Gracac by the officials of 3rd Police Station in Gracac area. Since Baricevic and Karamarko are members of the Croatian Army, the military police were called and the commander of the 71st Battalion of Military Police, Ivica Miletic, abated their receipts for cattle transportation, declaring them null and void. He told them to hand over the cattle to Civilian Protection. Then they were escorted to the Crime Service of the Military Police in Udbina, where they were told that receipts were valid and that they could go home with the cattle." And let me call for the third document. That is 65 ter 4523. And you can see, Mr. Matulovic, this is an order by the operational group -- commander of the Operational Group Zadar, Colonel [indiscernible]. It's dated 7th August, and it reads as follows: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Split Military District, dated 6th August, 1995, regarding supervision and proper handling of war booty, as well as efficient use of material supplies, I hereby order:" And if you could go to the next page, Madam Registrar, in the English translation only: "The 307th Logistics Base shall collect livestock and poultry on the liberated territory. "The collected livestock is to be put up in livestock farms or shall be sold straight away at market rates, which is more beneficial for the HV." And if I could have the final document on this series. Madam Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 2265, please. This is a letter sent by the assistant minister of interior, Mr. Josko Moric to all members of the military police -- all units of the members of the military police. And it's also drawn to the attention of the head of the Military Police Administration. And if you could turn on the English document, the next page. It reads: "Through monitoring the situation in the northern and southern part of the liberated area, it has been observed that certain representatives of the civilian government have been issuing certificates allowing citizens to enter and exit and even to take out movable property. The cases were also noted when those certificates were not even filled out, they were blank - so everyone could fill in the data on the property he is taking out." Next paragraph: "With regard to the above, the State Staff for Coordination of the Activities Concerning Return, Establishment of Civilian Authority and Normalisation of Life in the Newly-Liberated Areas ordered the chiefs of counties in newly-liberated areas to stop issuing such certificates and annulled previously issued certificates. All police administrations in the said area were given instructions regarding the treatment of persons in possession of these certificates, that is to say, the certificates should be confiscated and criminal offence should be determined. "I herewith submit the copy of the State Staff letter so the work and behaviour of the military police members can comply with it." Now, Mr. Matulovic, what we saw was the case file -- the first document was included in one of your case files where, in the official notes of interview, it was recorded the member of the HV who was charged had raised as his defence that he possessed a license to remove cattle. Then we saw a similar document, a second one, and this last document indicates that there were, in fact, licenses being issued to remove property from the liberated areas. Now, as a military court judge of the particular area, were you aware of this system by way of which licenses were being issued to either remove cattle or private property from the liberated area to members of the HV as well as other persons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start answering, I saw six or seven documents which pertained to completely different events. In the first document, it is confirmed that two persons are members of the HV, and then they go on to mention several cows, and then nine cows, and then cattle, and so on. And then you mentioned -- you showed me a document saying that it was some sort of a certificate, and it was no certificate. It was a criminal report, and in it, they said that it was crime 126, which is a serious case of theft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the documents shown to you have in common that in one way or another, reference is made to, whether we call it certificates or whether we call it -- at least documents which were apparently issued in order to legalise -- whether filled in already or not, to legalise transportation of goods. The question put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne was quite simple, whether you were aware of such documents being issued at the time. Or she even said a system of this kind of documents being issued. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about that because it didn't come under the jurisdiction of either civilian or military courts. These documents were issued in administrative proceedings, and those are quite separate proceedings. The documents were issued by administrative organs. And if those documents appeared in criminal proceedings, then they could argue that it was perhaps a forgery, a forgery by an employee of an administrative organ, and they could perhaps argue that it was an abuse of office and so on. Such a document existed in one of the cases, and it did not exculpate the person from appropriating a property if it was later established that it was not an abandoned property, but rather belonged to somebody. I would rather not go into any further legal analysis, but when it comes to these documents, how they were issued, how they were filled in or not filled in, whether the information filled in was accurate or not, I don't know. These documents are issued by administrative organs, and any questions concerning them should be addressed to the administrative organs. Military courts did not deal with such documents because they came nowhere near our jurisdiction. And if such documents, as I have said, emerged in a particular case, then, yes, they could pursue the matter further before civilian courts as to why somebody abused their office, somebody working in an administrative organ, and why did that person make a forgery of a document or issue the document beyond the scope of their authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I tender those four documents into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection based upon ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I look at page 81, lines 5 to 7. She cites from a document concerning these receipts: "Then they were escorted to the Crime Service of the Military Police in Udbina, where they were told that the receipts were valid and they could go home with the cattle." We had a witness here, the chief of the crime police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, perhaps could have spoken with personal knowledge of these documents. We bring him here so that they can address any issues they may have directly with a witness who has personal knowledge of them. The Court will recall that we spent three hours of cross-examination talking about the Blaskic case, and these types of matters weren't put to him. And now they're putting matters to a witness who says he doesn't know anything about this, didn't get copied on any of the documents, the documents don't indicate that he was copied on these matters. And then move them into evidence, where the Defence is now prejudiced, because a witness with relevant knowledge and authority doesn't have the opportunity to be confronted by the proposition that the Prosecution is trying to put in the case. We shouldn't have to now try to recall witnesses or call somebody else to address a matter that the Prosecution simply chose not to address with a competent witness, and we object under Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P2597, 2598, P2599, and P2600, all marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Mahindaratne, you'll be given an opportunity, before the witness leaves, to respond, if there's any need to do so, to what Mr. Misetic just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness apparently wants to raise an issue. Yes, Mr. Matulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I simply wanted to emphasise that a document is being put to me here, a document from Udbina, the 3rd Police Station. This was not our territory at all, so the court simply was not in a position to know about such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you testified that these kind of documents, you came across them, that you did not know much about who issued these, whether these were forgeries or not, but that at least that they did not convince your court that what seemed to be offences were suddenly no offences anymore because of these documents, if I just summarised briefly your testimony in this respect. And you are not aware of a system, you're not aware of -- and it is true, you're right in that, apparently, one of the examples dealt with a geographical area which might not have been within the area of competence of the Military Court in which this witness was serving.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take note of that, Mr. President. But may I just respond to Mr. Misetic's objection regarding breach of Rule 90(H) or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. An allegation of a rule -- breach of Rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 90(H) is -- we could -- we have another such one pending, but we could then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. We'll further consider also what you, at this moment, would like to argue in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would be obliged to place a matter before the witness under Rule 90(H), only if that witness testifies a contrary position to the position taken by the Prosecution. Now, the previous witness did not refer to looting or did not pursue any line of testimony which would require the Prosecution to place these documents before that witness. So I do not see -- there has not been a breach of Rule 90(H) in not placing these documents before the witness that Mr. Misetic has referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the objection mainly to be that it's unfair to put questions to witnesses in support of your own case, where a more relevant witness, who would have at least as much knowledge about the matter, was not questioned about it. It was not about the specific situation of Rule 90(H) under small "(iii)," I think Mr. Misetic referred to in its technical detail at the end of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness is also, in fact, a witness who could speak to these matters, because as we saw in the first document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Misetic did not challenge that. But he said you could not just select a couple of witnesses to which you put this material and do not pay any attention to it -- to witnesses who would have a similar or even better knowledge on the matter. Whether Mr. Misetic is right or wrong is another matter, but let's first try, at least, to understand what the objection is, and your responses - but, Mr. Misetic, correct me if I'm wrong - were responses to what apparently not the objection was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. The documents are marked for identification. Where the limits of the duty to put certain material to every witness are -- every witness which could testify about the matter will be further considered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just make one additional point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Exhibit P2597, MFI, also contains a judgement in which Mr. Matulovic was present. If there is something that the Prosecutor intends to contend about that judgement, it should be put to the witness while he's here. Nothing has been put to him about the judgement. I just want that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether you want to -- whether there is any such intention, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a transcript correction to be made. I called for a document which was 65 ter 3919A, but it has been recorded as "3918A." I just wanted to correct the record for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Matulovic, this is my last few questions for you. It is correct, isn't it, that you visited crime sites at the request of the military police or the military prosecutor? I beg your pardon, I made a mistake. I'm sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: A judge goes to the scene only if he's an investigative judge, if he's on duty, and if he's informed that an event containing elements of a crime occurred with serious consequences. So if he's informed by the military police that there was a traffic accident, where two cars collided, and there was minor damage, then he wouldn't go to the scene. But if it was a more serious crime, then it's the discretionary right of every investigative judge, including myself when I was doing this, to decide whether I would go out to the scene or not. I might go out to a scene when I received notification about the commission of a crime, where an investigative judge already went to the scene of a crime, if I assess that with my presence I could help with shedding light on this incident, give some professional advice, and help my colleague in his work. So whether I go out to the scene of the crime or not, it's the discretion of any judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you able to say as to about how many crime sites did you visit, an approximate figure, pursuant to the request of the military police in relation to killings of Serb civilians committed after August 5th to end of September 1995? Are you -- were you -- first of all, let me ask you, were you requested by the military police to visit any crime site of any killings committed by members of the HV of Serb civilians during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know this at all. If it was a crime scene of a murder, regardless of who that was, whether it was a Serb civilian or anyone else, then I would be duty-bound to go there because these were serious crimes, crimes of serious consequences. And if it was the territory that was under the jurisdiction of the Military Court in Split, then the persons who could go on the scene, because of the urgency of the procedure, and the collection of all traces, it could be the judge from Zadar, or the judge from Dubrovnik -- or the judge from Dubrovnik, or the judge from Split. So it was important that someone should go out onto the scene as soon as possible, because this warranted the quality of establishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters factual and simple. Were you ever -- did you ever go to a crime site for an on-site investigation in August and September 1995, as an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember now, personally I didn't do this. Perhaps I did, but as far as I can remember now, I did not. When did you say? In August and September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, it's of no use to ask you that if you have gone there, whether it was a murder case or not, because if you don't remember whether you went anywhere, you have no recollection as what kind of case you may have investigated. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall at least whether the military police requested you to visit any crime sites during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I said that military police could not request that. They did not have the authority to request a judge to go out to a crime site. If it was something more serious, they had the obligation to inform a judge, and then a judge would decide whether he would go out to the crime site or not, and he had the discretion to make this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you informed by the military police of any particular crime which required you to visit a crime site during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of crime sites do you have in mind, what crimes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me be very specific. Killings of civilians, burning or destruction to private property, and I believe you would not be required to visit sites for theft, so those specific types of crimes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Only about murders. Even now, investigative judges do not go to crime scenes if these were fires or arsons, regardless of the amount of damage that may have been caused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have document number 7348, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'd like to seek clarification of the last answer. You said "only about murders." You then referred to being informed by the military police of murders on which you could have considered whether or not to go to the crime site; is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but precisely as I answered the question of Ms. Mahindaratne. She asked me whether I went out to the crime scenes, and then she listed three crimes; murder, arson and aggravated theft. And I said, of these three, it was only murders where one was duty-bound to go out to the crime scene and be present during the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't come as a surprise that this confusion does exist. You told us when you were duty-bound to go there. Can I conclude from that, that since you told us that you have no recollection of ever going to a crime site as an investigative judge, that you never received any report from the military police of murder because you told us that under those circumstances you would have been obliged to go there, or that at least you have no recollection of ever having received a report on a murder that had been committed? Is that a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, mostly, yes, though I wish to be more specific. All the reports after -- made after an information that there was a -- a murder was committed would not be sent to a judge, but to a military prosecutor or a civilian prosecutor, who then determines what steps would be taken next and how this case would be handled later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would then the conclusion be fair that you never received any request from a military prosecutor to go and investigate the crime scene in relation to murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military prosecutor simultaneously receives information about the commission of a crime, simultaneously with the investigative judge, and the two of them, after having received the report, try to communicate and to agree who would do what. And if the investigative judge decides to go onto the crime scene, then it's the obligation of the military prosecutor to go with him there, too, because the military prosecutor also is involved in the criminal procedure later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you about reports received from the military police, and now you tell us that a military prosecutor simultaneously receives information about the commission of a crime, simultaneously with the investigative judge, which at least leaves it open that you did receive. Now, apart from what the system was, did you, in August and September 1995, receive information by the police, either directly or through the military prosecutor, about a murder being committed on the basis of which you have considered whether or not you were duty-bound to go to that crime scene for investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I emphasise if it was a murder, there was no consideration. One had to go, regardless of who informed the investigative judge about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not an answer to my question, that even if you were duty-bound to go, then you consider whether you were duty-bound, and the answer then is, Yes. I would like to know, and apparently Ms. Mahindaratne as well, is whether you ever received any murder reports under those circumstances, not what the system was, whether you were -- you had to consider, but what did you receive? Did you ever receive any murder reports --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- directly or indirectly -- you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember it, or you did not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember at all that I received any reports about any murders, and even less so whether I was in doubt whether I should go out to the crime scene or not. If they were murders, then one had to go. Let me repeat that once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, how about arson or burning; were you ever informed or requested by the military police or the military prosecutors to visit a crime site of an incident of burning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that arson, as an offence, was not covered by the obligation to go out to the crime scene, regardless of whether these were military prosecutors or civilian prosecutors or judges. One had to go to the on-site investigations only when these were serious criminal offences. So if it was arson, it could be a house that was set on fire, but without great damage being inflicted, it could have been hay that was on fire, and the number of us was small. And in such huge territory, it wasn't necessary for us to go to the on-site investigation for such crimes.
