We let the police or military police do this and determine whether the persons were still active servicemen or not, or they used to be and were not anymore, so they were processed regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you see, Mr. Matulovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, again I'd like to clearly understand the answer. Do I have to understand your answer to be that you may well have received such information about burnings, but that for the reasons you explained, you would not have -- this would not have triggered you to go to the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, at the same time there was a reason for the military prosecutor to continue with the procedure to process this and to monitor the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the end of the story, but at that moment there was no need to go there. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President. I called up a document, but in view of the last answer, it's not necessary for me to tender that document into evidence. Mr. Matulovic, thank you for answering my questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Any need for re-examination? Mr. Misetic. Oh, and, yes, I'm looking at the clock. Nevertheless, I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It depends on -- if we're coming back tomorrow with the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that depends to some extent on your answer as well, isn't it? That's chicken and egg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would have about two questions for the witness, which may take five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Matulovic, you were asked some questions about disciplinary measures. Let me just ask you: At the conclusion of a criminal case, if there were a conviction, would the court -- would your court then refer the matter to the military for a disciplinary proceeding to begin, or what would happen once the conviction was entered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Once a person was convicted, I already said that one copy of the judgement would be sent to the unit and also to the Ministry of Defence. The issuing of the judgement meant that a person was found guilty, but this was not necessarily a condition that the question of disciplinary responsibility would be raised in the unit. It could be, but not necessarily, if the commander of the unit decided that the soldier was found guilty and convicted of this offence. I emphasise that there were disciplinary infractions and also disciplinary offences. For the disciplinary offences, the military prosecutor was responsible, and he decided about the disciplinary procedure. And for disciplinary infractions, that was the direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. I have only a few questions, and with the indulgence of the interpreters and transcribers, I think we can finish in five minutes, and the courtroom is empty this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 3, you quote Article 6 of the decree which defines the jurisdiction of military courts only in criminal cases, and I re-read the last portion; that is, to -- no, I'll -- no, I'll withdraw that question. I have only one question of a rather general nature. If a commander receives information, and I'm talking about a higher-ranking commander, that in his area of responsibility arson is committed, although he does not get every detail, but let's say he receives information that houses were set ablaze in several villages, but if this information is rather diffuse, in view of the duty of a commander to take necessary and reasonable measures to punish any serious violations of international humanitarian law, what would have been, in your view, apart from instructions that it should not happen again through the chain of command, but what would have been the available avenues to take care that he did what was necessary and reasonable to achieve that the perpetrators would be punished? What should he do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: If a commander, regardless of the level of his command, might assess all this, he had to be at least a lawyer. He would have to know the Criminal Code and everything else that relates to criminal offences. Therefore, in my view, a commander, once he received information as a layman who doesn't know much about law, should inform the military police that it should urgently act, establish all the facts in relation to a certain act, unlawful action that was carried out in this area, that he indirectly learned about. So he wasn't an eye-witness of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could a commander, and let's assume a military district commander, give orders to the military police to investigate such allegations of crimes committed by possibly members of his forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the direct chain of command, he could only inform the military police about this, and the military police existed for this purpose as a group of professionals who are in charge of criminal processing. And even without his information, if they had some information about this, they would automatically carry out some activities in order to find the perpetrators and to prosecute them. This is why the Military Police Administration existed, and battalions. They were professionals, they were lawyers as a rule, and they had specific knowledge how to act automatically in such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in case they couldn't find the time or if they had set priorities which were not in accordance with the priorities the commander considered the right ones, what else than just informing the military police could the commander do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MATULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't do anything, because information sent to military police automatically meant -- and now we can talk about the orders, as I did about the orders and the instructions at the beginning of my testimony, the order to do so, and take action to uncover the perpetrators and the acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. If the questions by the Bench have not triggered any further need to put questions to the witness, Mr. Matulovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. And I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions put to you by the Bench and by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the witness is released, given his responses, we would be wondering whether that would trigger a Rule 90(H) obligation on our part to put the Prosecution case to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I never learned that questions by the -- oh, you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The answers, Mr. President, the responses by the witness to the questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that no obligation arises from any questions by the Bench to put the case of the Prosecution or of the Defence to the witness. At least that's -- if there's any misunderstanding about that, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just sought your guidance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it would also suggest that the witness is cross-examined by the Bench, which is, in my view, not the case, Ms. Mahindaratne. Since I hear no further support for your suggestion, I would refrain from it and continue to thank the witness for having answered all the questions, and I wish you a safe return home again, Mr. Matulovic. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to thank the interpreters and the transcribers very much for making it possible for the witness to finish his testimony today. We adjourn, and I received a note in which courtroom we would continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do not have a witness tomorrow. We had this witness scheduled for today and tomorrow. And our next witness, which is General Cross, an expert, doesn't arrive until tomorrow afternoon for Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not for the first time that I express now, on behalf of the Chamber, our concern about these matters. Not to say that I do understand the difficulties in scheduling, but at the same time, it has happened too often. Have you discussed the matter with the Prosecution, how much time they think they would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have not discussed it with the Prosecution on how much time they need. General Cross simply -- well, he had an operation, number one, without going into the personal details of that, and couldn't come sooner, and then had professional obligations. And this was the first available time that we could get him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the same happens in September. And I think you received a -- you received an e-mail about that. Scheduling, without even considering what the other party would do, is a useless exercise. It's just a simple matter of court management. If you say, We schedule two days for the witness, and if you take one hour and a half, as Mr. Misetic did, one hour and -- close to two hours, then of course everything depends on what the Cermak Defence, what the Markac Defence, and what the Prosecution does. So, therefore, if you're talking about an efficient use of our time in court, this is a minimal requirement, I would say, in order to make any useful scheduling. I do understand that I can't change the situation for tomorrow, and I do understand that if Mr. Cross would have been -- undergo surgery one day earlier, that the whole problem would not have existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have tried to efficiently use the Court's time, and I think that we, to date, have done so, barring an event here and there. But with regard to this instance, my apologies, Mr. President, and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not that we feel so much -- we have court available, we have interpreters available, we have court staff available, and even if we take minimal time, then the next question is: How are we going to use the time that remains? And it's mainly in respect of that problem that the Chamber is a bit concerned about the developments. At the same time, the Chamber also appreciates that the conclusion of the Gotovina Defence case will most likely take place in early September, but we have now asked those questions to the parties. We'll resume, then, on Thursday, the 23rd of July, at quarter past 2.00 in the -- quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
